title: Australia's Parties Need the Indian Diaspora Vote. The Immigration Debate Is Bruising It.
excerpt: A Coalition senator's claim that Labor imports Indian voters forced her own leader into damage control, in a community of 916,000 whose outer-suburban seats decide elections.
body:
• Australia's Indian diaspora numbers about 916,000 India-born residents, the country's second-largest overseas-born group, and both major parties need its vote in western Sydney and Melbourne seats.
  • Polling cited by the ABC puts Indian-Australian support for Labor at 75-85% in some areas; a Carnegie survey cited in parliament put it at 43% Labor to 26% Coalition.
  • Coalition senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price claimed Labor imports migrants who vote for it, singling out Indians, then refused to apologise, forcing Opposition Leader Sussan Ley into damage control.
  • Community members say the immigration debate, and anti-immigration rallies days earlier, have left many feeling singled out.

Labor and the Coalition both need the Indian diaspora vote. Australia's immigration debate is making that vote harder to hold. About 916,000 people born in India live in Australia, the second-largest overseas-born group in the country, concentrated in exactly the outer-suburban seats that decide federal elections.

The Remark That Started It

Coalition senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price told ABC Radio that Labor allows in migrants who "support their policies" and vote for the government, pointing to the Indian diaspora as her example, according to AAP. The comments came days after mass anti-immigration rallies attended by neo-Nazis, at which promotional flyers used false claims to fuel anti-Indian rhetoric.

Price declined to apologise. "I don't believe I have anything to apologise about," she told reporters in Canberra. Opposition Leader Sussan Ley was left to repair the damage: "I'm fighting for every single Australian, no matter where you came from, and our Australian Indian community are amazing," Ley told Sky News. Shadow Attorney-General Julian Leeser said the Coalition believed in a "race-blind" migration policy.

What the Numbers Actually Say

The voting picture is strong for Labor but not monolithic. Pollster Kos Samaras has estimated 75-85% of Indian Australians in some regions backed Labor at the last federal election, the ABC reported via Europe Says. A Carnegie Endowment survey cited by Labor MP Andrew Charlton put identification at 43% for Labor against 26% for the Coalition.

Sukhmani Khorana, an associate professor at the University of New South Wales, found a strong Labor primary vote in western Sydney suburbs with large Indian populations, including Parramatta, Westmead, Wentworthville and Girraween, but noted some areas favoured the Liberals, with differences by class, occupation and time of migration.

How It Feels on the Ground

In Harris Park, Sydney's Little India, locals told SBS the remarks left them feeling unfairly targeted. Ritwik Singh, whose father migrated on a skilled visa, rejected Price's claim: "Indian people tend to vote by looking at their backyard. They're looking at what's most important for them." Voters interviewed by the ABC named housing affordability, childcare and affordable healthcare as the issues that decided their votes.

Khorana said part of Labor's support reflects a reaction against the scapegoating of migrants and international students, including rhetoric linking immigration to the housing crisis.

What's Next

Analysts warn the Labor lean is not permanent: second and third-generation migrants in other communities have historically drifted toward the Coalition over time. For now, both parties face the same arithmetic. A community this large, in seats this marginal, cannot be courted and bruised at the same time.
